requirements.statement: The last navigation item, 'Log out', links to /auth/sign-out on every frontend (animals, INS and plants) and is never marked as the current item. Log out ends the user's session with the service and sends them to Defra ID's sign-out page, headed 'You have signed out'. Opening the dashboard again afterwards asks them to sign in again with their user ID and password. A user who is not signed in and opens /auth/sign-out goes to the service root.
requirements.why: Ending a real session properly is an authentication behaviour the prototype cannot show. It already works and is proven end to end.
requirements.deltaNote: The item links to /auth/sign-out on all three frontends (repo-frontend-p2-010, repo-insfrontend-p4-010, repo-plantsfrontend-p13-007). trace-e2e-p1-041 to p1-046 and repo-tests-p6-073 show Log out reaching the signed-out page and the dashboard asking for sign-in again (repo-tests-p6-075); repo-insfrontend-p4-096 to p4-098 give the INS routes. One security spec holds the only check that the INS front door renders the link, and it reads 'Log out' (repo-tests-p15-104, p15-105, p16-125).

requirements.why: The target design shows Manage account as a placeholder with no destination, which is what all three frontends do today, and the earlier parity programme recorded that the item has no owner or destination to point at.

requirements.statement: The first navigation item, Dashboard, links to the dashboard home of the set or frontend the page belongs to and is marked as the current item there. On the animals frontend it links to the set's own root (/live-animals for live-animals), which renders that set's own notification list, and stays current on every page inside a notification, because the list, the create action and everything under them count as one section. On the plants frontend it links to the plants set's own root and stays current on every notification page. On the INS frontend it links to / and is current only there. A Back, 'View dashboard' or 'Return to your dashboard' link that the target design sends to the overall dashboard goes to the set's own notification list.
requirements.why: In the target design the dashboard is the home: it is the Dashboard item's target and where the back link to the dashboard goes. The owner's 9 October afternoon and templates rulings keep each notification list in its own frontend at the set root, so the item and every return to the dashboard stay on the set root, which all three frontends already link to.
requirements.deltaNote: The animals Dashboard item goes to the page's home URL and stays current while the dashboard section is active (repo-frontend-p2-009, p2-013, p2-130, trace-e2e-p9-083); the plants item goes to the set's own base URL and the list and create URLs under it count as the dashboard section (repo-plantsfrontend-p13-007, p13-010, p13-069); the INS item goes to / and is current only there (repo-insfrontend-p4-007, p4-012, trace-e2e-p15-002). Each set root keeps rendering its own list (ruling-sam-2026-10-09-pm-p3-089, p3-103), so nothing moves. Where each return link points is built by the areas that own those pages (ruling-sam-2026-10-09-pm-p3-101).

requirements.statement: On every frontend, a page shows a GOV.UK back link labelled 'Back' ('Yn ôl' in Welsh), above the page content, only when it supplies somewhere for it to go. No page shows breadcrumbs, even when breadcrumbs are passed to the layout. On the animals and plants frontends Back goes to the place the trader actually came from, carried between pages in a 'from' query parameter listing those places newest last and holding at most 40 of them; a trail naming anywhere the journey does not have is ignored in full and Back falls back to the notification's overview, or to the place the page names instead. A page opened from another page returns to it when the request carries a 'return' marker naming a page allowed to open it, and a marker naming anything else is ignored. The trail and the return marker are percent-encoded into the address and join a query string the address already has.
requirements.why: Each page gets one route back (the back link) and one route up (the service navigation), and the trail is what makes the back link lead where the trader came from rather than to a fixed page. This already exists.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-frontend-p2-017, repo-insfrontend-p4-018 and repo-plantsfrontend-p13-016 render the back link only when one is set, and repo-plantsfrontend-p13-017 shows breadcrumbs are never rendered. repo-frontend-p2-054 to p2-059 and repo-plantsfrontend-p13-073 to p13-079 give the trail, its 40-place cap and the return marker; repo-tests-p16-094 and p16-094-m1 show the end-to-end suite asserts a trail from the page objects' own slugs rather than typing one.

requirements.statement: A journey page on the animals frontend names its section in a caption directly above its heading, such as 'About the consignment' above 'Main reason for import', in the large GOV.UK caption size, and shows nothing where the journey leaves the page uncaptioned. Where the question legend is visually hidden, the caption still sits directly above the page heading. The dashboard has an extra-large 'Dashboard' caption above its heading, and the overview has no caption. The plants frontend shows its journey pages' section caption the same way and may ask for another caption size.
requirements.why: Section captions already exist on both journey frontends, derived from where the page sits in the journey. No source in this area's working set from the target design says otherwise.
requirements.deltaNote: trace-animals-fit-p1-007 to p1-012 show the captions as rendered, repo-frontend-p2-032 and p2-033 how they are derived, and repo-plantsfrontend-p13-059 and p13-060 the plants captions. Each page's own caption wording against the target design belongs to that page's area.

Each has a Welsh twin, and a page's own message wins over them.

requirements.statement: On the animals and plants frontends, a save that hits a recoverable backend failure re-renders the page with an alert banner titled 'There is a problem' that reads 'Sorry, there is a problem with the service. Your answers on this page have been saved. Try again in a few minutes.' The banner sits at the top of the content column, and the page carries on working.
requirements.why: Real persistence can fail, which the prototype cannot express. The banner tells the user their answers are safe.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-frontend-p2-021 and p2-051 render the banner on animals, and repo-plantsfrontend-p13-019 and p13-064 on plants, where it is announced as an alert and sits first in the content column (repo-plantsfrontend-p13-019-m1).

requirements.statement: On the INS frontend, a page whose service call fails is re-rendered with status 500 and a notification banner with role 'alert', titled 'There is a problem' and reading 'Sorry, there is a problem with the service. Try again in a few minutes.'
requirements.why: Real upstream services can fail, which the prototype cannot express, and the user is kept on the page.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-insfrontend-p4-020 and p4-021 render the banner.

requirements.statement: On the animals and plants frontends, a form post refused because the notification changed after the page was opened sends the user back to the same page, keeping any trail the address carried. There an alert banner titled 'The notification has been updated' reads 'This notification was updated since you opened it. Review the details and try again.' Every page of a notification carries the token that says which version of it the trader is looking at, and a stale refusal is passed on as a stale refusal rather than shown as a brief backend failure.
requirements.why: Concurrent edits to a stored notification are a persistence constraint the prototype cannot express, and the user must be told rather than shown a generic failure.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-frontend-p2-022, p2-052 and p2-053 implement the refusal, the marker and the banner on animals, and repo-plantsfrontend-p13-020, p13-061, p13-062 and p13-094-m1 on plants.

requirements.statement: A page inside a notification can show a shared strip above its content with the notification's status tag and its reference in bold, the reference being the notification's own journey id: blue 'Draft', green 'Submitted', yellow for an amendment or grey 'Deleted'. While the notification is being amended the strip also offers a 'Cancel amend' link to that notification's cancel-amend page, and a page can switch that link off while keeping the strip, or leave the strip off altogether and draw its own header in the set's template. The strip is shared by every set on the animals and plants frontends and is not reworded in place except by the Amend bar. The INS layout supports the strip, but no INS page uses it.
requirements.why: This is shared page chrome that already exists. The afternoon ruling keeps it as it is for every set: a page that needs another header switches it off, and only the Amend bar changes it in place. Each page's use of it belongs to that page's area.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-frontend-p2-023 to p2-025 and repo-plantsfrontend-p13-021 to p13-026 render the strip, its tag and its Cancel amend link, and a page can leave it out (repo-insfrontend-p4-022, repo-plantsfrontend-p13-025, ruling-sam-2026-10-09-pm-p2-061).

In Welsh the title and heading read 'Mae'n ddrwg gennym, ni allwn eich mewngofnodi', with 'Rhowch' before the link 'gynnig arall arni'.

The page has no back link. It is shown when the Defra ID callback fails, the token carries no organisation or fails verification, or the user's role and permissions cannot be loaded.
requirements.why: These are authentication failures the prototype cannot express, and the page already exists.

requirements.statement: An error response on every frontend is shown as the shared error page with the error's own HTTP status. The page's large heading is the status number, and a paragraph below it, which is also the browser title, reads 'Page not found' (404), 'Forbidden' (403), 'You need to sign in to view this page' (401), 'There is a problem with your request' (400) or 'Something went wrong' (any other). Its content holds only that heading and message: no back link and no error summary, with the service navigation still there for a signed-in user. A notification that cannot be found shows that standard page not found, like every other page in the service. An error on a path inside a journey set, routed or not, uses that set's chrome; a path under no set uses set-free chrome whose home link is the site root and which shows no status strip, no success banner and no recoverable-error banner.
requirements.why: Real errors are a constraint the prototype cannot express, and every frontend already shares this page; the owner's 19 November ruling makes a missing notification take it too.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-frontend-p2-029 and p2-030, repo-insfrontend-p4-072 to p4-078 and repo-plantsfrontend-p13-053, p13-054 and p13-055-m1 render the page; repo-plantsfrontend-p13-057 and p13-058 and repo-frontend-p2-135-m1 decide which set's chrome an error takes; repo-tests-p10-111 and p15-073 scan the 404 page. The ruling's missing-notification clause is the only part not yet proven for the review page (ruling-sam-2026-11-19-p1-030).

After a copy, a success message titled 'Notification copied' reads 'A new draft notification has been created.' After a delete, one titled 'Notification deleted' reads 'The notification has been deleted.' Each has a Welsh twin. requirements.statement: Address pickers offer a shared 'Add a new address' link, and a success banner titled 'Success' says the named address was added to your address book. When a chosen address is not in the user's address book, the error reads 'The address could not be found in your address book. Select another address or try adding it again.' When the address book cannot be reached, it reads 'The address book could not be reached. Your answers on this page have been saved. Try again in a few minutes.'

requirements.statement: Sign-in hands off to Defra ID with an OpenID Connect authorisation-code request (scope openid offline_access, query response mode, policy b2c_1a_cui_cpdev_signupsigninsfi), naming each frontend's own serviceId and its own /auth/sign-in-oidc callback. On success, the user's organisation, CRN and name are taken from the token and held in a server-side session.
requirements.why: Real sign-in through Defra ID is an authentication constraint the prototype's sign-in page cannot express.
requirements.deltaNote: trace-e2e-p1-002 to p1-004 and trace-e2e-p15-012 record the handoff.

requirements.statement: After signing in, a user who belongs to more than one organisation is asked to 'Choose your organisation' from radios labelled with each organisation's name and SBI, with a Continue button. A user with one organisation never sees that choice. The chosen organisation reaches the service through the sign-in callback, and the user lands on the page they asked for. No page in the service offers a way to switch organisation, and a page that needs an organisation returns 403 when the session has none.
requirements.why: Organisation choice is part of real Defra ID authentication, which the prototype cannot express.
requirements.deltaNote: trace-e2e-p15-016 to p15-020 record the single-organisation and multi-organisation paths on the INS frontend, repo-tests-p6-080 and p14-083 the picker's heading and options, and repo-tests-p16-163 to p16-165 the two identities the suite signs in as, one of them in two organisations.

requirements.statement: Signing in to one frontend signs the user in to the others without asking for credentials again, because Defra ID answers their requests straight away. Each frontend keeps its own session cookie on the shared host (sid for animals, ins-sid for INS, plants-sid for plants, unless a run names one), so all three sessions are kept side by side, and the three homes sit at different paths. Each service has its own landing page after sign-in, the INS frontend's checked landing page being the address book.
requirements.why: Moving between the animals journey and the INS dashboard and address book is cross-service behaviour the prototype cannot express. It already works.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p14-078 to p14-081 and trace-e2e-p15-111 and p15-113 prove single sign-on and kept sessions across the three frontends from a browser with no cookies, and repo-tests-p16-055 shows a new context can carry only the auth cookie so no journey state travels with it.

requirements.statement: A session is valid only while it is in the server-side cache (Redis when deployed). The session cookie lasts 4 hours and is HttpOnly. An expired token is refreshed when refresh is on, and otherwise the user is treated as signed out. Every route needs a signed-in user unless it opts out, on the request that shows a page and on the request that saves it alike.
requirements.why: Real sessions are an authentication constraint the prototype cannot express, and they already work this way.
requirements.deltaNote: trace-e2e-p1-031 and p1-032 record the cookies, repo-insfrontend-p4-102 and p4-103 the session rules and repo-plantsfrontend-p13-033-m1 that both the show and the save request need a session. What a user sees when a session lapses is not recorded (trace-e2e-p1-062).

requirements.statement: In stub mode the INS frontend signs a user in at once with no sign-in page, as 'Stub User' in the organisation given by an organisationId parameter (default 'stub-org-1'). The stub session lasts four hours, sign-out goes straight to /, and the Defra ID callback and organisation routes do not exist. Stub mode is refused in production.
requirements.why: This is how the INS frontend runs locally and in its own browser tests. It is part of today's real authentication set-up.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-insfrontend-p4-106 to p4-113 give the stub mode.

requirements.statement: On every frontend, every form post must carry a valid CSRF token (except under /health, /assets and /public). Every page carries the token in a csrf-token meta tag in its head, every form has a hidden 'crumb' input, and the CSRF cookie is HttpOnly and SameSite Strict.
requirements.why: Protection against cross-site request forgery is a real security constraint, and it already exists.

requirements.statement: The animals frontend sends a Content-Security-Policy on its pages, redirects and sign-in callback. It limits scripts, styles, fonts, images and the base URL to its own origin (plus one hashed inline script), lets forms post to itself and the address book origin, and forbids framing and plugins. It also sends Strict-Transport-Security for a year, X-Frame-Options DENY, X-Content-Type-Options nosniff, X-Download-Options noopen, X-XSS-Protection and Cache-Control no-cache.

requirements.statement: The tests repo's accessibility suite holds every scanned page to WCAG 2.2 AA. Every test carries the @a11y tag and is reported under that standard, read from the fixture so the title and the rule set cannot drift apart, and every scan passes the five axe tags wcag2a, wcag2aa, wcag21a, wcag21aa and wcag22aa explicitly, because axe's own default leaves target-size out. A scan waits for the DOM and then allows a bounded settling period, scanning anyway if that wait times out; it is recorded against the page's path; a test runs every one of its scans before failing and reports them together with each violation's severity, rule, description, node count and help link, attaching them to the report as JSON; a failing scan fails its test and a test that takes the scan but never runs one fails too. A test is allowed five minutes. Pages whose layout matters at small sizes are scanned again at 320 by 568 and at 568 by 320, and a narrow scan also proves the page does not scroll sideways once its tables are discounted. A scan may be narrowed per page, and the only exclusions are the two conditional-reveal radio groups whose aria-expanded attribute axe rejects and the sign-in stub's own error list: upstream disagreements in code the service does not own. A clean scan is not full conformance, and a state earns its own scan only where its value outweighs the set-up it needs.
requirements.why: Every page this programme changes must keep passing this suite, and a new scan has to be written to these rules. It already exists.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p10-001 to p10-022 and p15-058 to p15-060 define the suite, p10-142 to p10-144 and p15-080 to p15-082 prove the scanner itself catches a real fault, and p10-013 to p10-017, p15-091 and p16-029 give the only exclusions.

The organisation-scoped API refusals are proven by status code only, the sign-in error is proven only for present-but-invalid values, no test drives the organisation picker as a journey of its own, and nothing proves another organisation's user is refused a notification's view page as well as its overview.

requirements.statement: The tests repo's security suite is a traffic-driven OWASP ZAP scan of six services, each its own named ZAP context with its own address: the animals frontend, the animals admin, the INS frontend, the animals backend, the plants backend and the address book. Playwright drives real signed-in journeys through the proxy rather than letting ZAP crawl, so coverage is traffic-driven and the attacking corpus is curated by hand. There are two profiles: a passive one that runs the end-to-end suite without attacking, and an attacking one that runs only the @active corpus, is deliberate, runs on the compose stack alone and is refused on the deployed platform because its journeys delete records the scan then re-fires with fuzzed payloads. Anything but the exact attacking profile name is treated as passive. Identifiers in a page or API address are declared to ZAP as data rather than structure, from a context plan registered before any traffic exists; all three plans must declare the same contexts; diagnostics are excluded rather than scanned; the DOM cross-site-scripting rule is off; the uploader and the queue-consuming INS backend are out of scope with their reasons; and the three APIs are scanned because every API client inherits the run's proxy. The attacking corpus drives sign-in and sign-out, a whole submitted journey, the reason-gated pages and a private transporter, amend, copy, cancel and delete, a document upload with its scan and download, a draft validation error, the notification list's search, paging and sorting, the review page's Change trail, and the INS address book's whole record lifecycle with its role filter, its refused hand-off guard and the INS dashboard. A run fails on a FAIL-rated alert from the rules file (an unlisted alert failing only if it is high risk), on a scan that finished at or within half a minute of its 60-minute cap, or on a declared context that saw no traffic; a per-domain run gates only that domain's contexts and is labelled scoped, and an unknown domain is refused by name. Each run clears its report folder but never removes it, writes a landing page before failing with a row per site, its request count and alert counts, publishes ZAP's log and machine-readable report as HTML, and the pass-or-fail decision is made by the suite's own gate rather than by the plans.
requirements.why: Every route this programme adds or changes must be driven through this scan to be attacked, and a new spec has to be written to these rules. The suite already exists.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p11-037 to p11-102, p15-094 to p15-116 and p16-106 to p16-134 define the suite, its profiles, its contexts, its corpus and its three failure conditions; p16-144 to p16-148 give how a deployed run starts ZAP itself and publishes its report.

requirements.statement: The tests repo signs each worker in once per domain and its tests restore that session, the saved state holding only the auth cookie and never written until a fresh context has proved it restores to a signed-in landing page; a spec that must start unauthenticated opts out with a cold-start state, and session reuse can be switched off, which caps the deployed run's workers. Only the session cookie is carried between a worker's tests, so each test starts signed in with no part-answered notification. Reuse was proved against one deployed environment by a probe that mints one session and reuses it across twenty fresh contexts, refuses to run against production, and is to be re-run before relying on reuse elsewhere. The sign-in password comes from the environment with a local stub default and is never written into a trace, the sign-in fixtures have their own longer timeout, no spec wipes the database because every spec creates the state it asserts on, and only internet-bound calls go through the platform's proxy.
requirements.why: Any new end-to-end proof of sign-in or navigation has to work within these existing suite rules.

requirements.statement: The performance suite signs in as a browser does: it follows a frontend's redirect chain through that frontend's /auth/sign-in, the Defra ID stub's sign-in form (posting the stub identity's CRN 2100010101 and a password) and /auth/callback back to the page asked for. It tags the post 'sign-in' and any later sign-in as re-authentication, checks that the INS sign-in went through Defra ID, and shares one cookie jar between the INS frontend and the journey frontend so the INS sign-in carries over to the live-animals dashboard.

A stale concurrency token answered with a redirect counts as handled, and a request that is still redirecting after 10 hops fails its check.

requirements.statement: The plants set is mounted at /high-risk-plants, every plants link carries that prefix, and every plants page renders in the shared layout, loading one application stylesheet and one application script module. A set must mount at a path starting with a slash and must configure everything the platform requires of it, or it is refused at mount with the missing piece and the call that would supply it named. Where only one set is mounted, pages built outside a request still resolve to it. A page inside a set renders through the layout that set names, so a set can give its own pages different chrome.

requirements.statement: Every page of the animals and plants journey frontends carries a page-maturity banner, a second phase banner directly under the Alpha one and above the Back link, saying how settled the page's design is. The four states read 'Exploring' ('This page is an early idea. It may change a lot or be removed.'), 'Detailing' ('We're keeping this page. We're still working out the detail.'), 'Agreed' ('Users and the business have agreed this page. Changes need a reason.') and 'Ready for live' ('This page is ready for live.'), with an orange, purple, teal or green tag and the banner row behind it in the same colour at a lighter tint. A page that says nothing about how settled it is shows as Exploring. A screen reader hears 'This page's status:' before the tag and a full stop after it. The banner is left off an error page and off any response that is not a page of the journey, the whole banner can be switched off for an environment and is on by default, and its prefix and all four states have Welsh copy with the same keys as the English. A page's maturity travels with its route.
requirements.why: The maturity banner is how a reader of a page can tell whether its design is settled, which the prototype has no way to express and says nothing about. It already exists on both journey frontends and nothing in the target design or the rulings removes it.

requirements.statement: The tests repo's visual-regression suite guards rendered composition: layout, spacing, colour and typography as the user sees a page, by comparing screenshots against committed baselines and failing when pixels differ outside the masked regions. Every spec carries the @visual tag and forces a headless browser for itself, because headed mode uses the operating system's own font rendering; on macOS the browser is launched with always-shown scroll bars and a coarse pointer so a Mac shot matches the Linux baseline. Each shot is committed twice, once for each platform, and both are regenerated when a visual change is intended, the Linux ones from a container that reaches the stack by its host name. A shot is taken at 1280 by 1000 pixels unless the test resizes the viewport. Content that moves with the clock or the run is pinned: a full-page shot of a notification page masks the whole status strip rather than the reference alone, so the masked box stays a fixed size, while the notification view and declaration shots overwrite the reference number and the dates with fixed text; a calendar shot stops the browser clock on a fixed day and moves the served earliest and latest dates by the same number of days. Only the animals and plants domains have visual specs.
requirements.why: A change to shared page chrome is exactly what this suite exists to catch, so every chrome change this programme makes either keeps the baselines or regenerates both platforms' baselines in the same increment.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p11-001 to p11-010 and p16-096 to p16-105 define the suite, its dual baselines, its headless and macOS rules, its viewport and its masks; repo-tests-p16-102 and p16-102-m1 give the two regeneration commands.

requirements.statement: Which pages and states the visual suite pins, and its coverage gaps, are weighed where those pages are weighed: the origin page on first load and with its region code revealed, the import reason page in its transhipment, transit, temporary admission, error and no-JavaScript states, the arrival details page, the transited countries page empty and with one country, the identification card, the accompanying documents page with one scanned document, the consignor picker's search row, the arrival date picker's button at rest, hovered and focused and its calendar opened by mouse and by keyboard, the overview's totals, the notification view as review at desktop width, the refused review at desktop and phone width and the declaration. No baseline covers the germinal-products set, the notification list, the confirmation page, the commodity pages, the address book or the INS front door, and the review has a desktop baseline but no phone one.
requirements.why: Each baseline pins one page's own composition, so the page's area weighs it against the target design; the missing baselines are gaps in today's suite rather than differences from the design, and go to the report.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p11-011 to p11-036 and p11-109 list the baselines, and p11-103 and p11-104 the gaps.

requirements.statement: The tests repo has exactly two targets, the deployed services and the docker-compose stack, one config file each, extending one shared config that holds the projects, the reporters, one retry and a trace on the first retry with a screenshot only on failure. One default project, chromium, runs every domain, and five opt-in projects run only when named: branded Chrome, Firefox, WebKit, an emulated iPhone 17 and an emulated Pixel 10. The four desktop projects render at 1280 by 1000 and the two mobile ones take their device's viewport. A deployed run gives each test 60 seconds and each expectation 15 seconds because each page load is a real network hop, a compose run keeps Playwright's defaults, and a test that needs longer sets its own. Each flow step waits up to 30 seconds for its page's heading so a transient gateway error fails the step that hit it and names the page. Tests run fully in parallel, a run on CI refuses a test marked only, and how many browsers run at once is capped by a setting that takes a whole number or a percentage and stops the run with both accepted forms when it is anything else. Every run refuses to start against production, a missing service base URL or a domain with no base URL stops the run naming what was missing, a compose run from a workspace clone that does not own the stack stops before the first test unless told to carry on, and a containerised compose run adds a host-resolver rule so the stack's localhost redirects resolve. Local service ports and deployed per-service subdomains are fixed, back-end calls from a laptop go through the protected gateway with a developer API key over the department's VPN, and the shared settings file is import-only so an editor does not offer it as a runnable config.
requirements.why: Any new end-to-end, accessibility or visual proof this programme adds runs under these settings, and a change that needs a new route, port or longer budget has to be made here.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-025 to p16-033 and p16-068 to p16-078 give the configs, the projects, the timeouts, the retries and the guards; p16-060 to p16-067-m1 the addresses of every service on both targets.

requirements.statement: The tests repo is run by named scripts, one per suite and target, and by a profile on the deployed platform. Locally there are end-to-end, accessibility, visual, cross-browser, BrowserStack, passive-security and scoped active-security runs against the compose stack, a CI script for the workspace stack job, and the same set against the deployed services, with per-domain copies of each that limit the run to that domain's own directory and are named to match the platform's profiles. A dash in the per-domain table means that domain has no specs of that test type yet. A deployed run picks its suite with a profile value, an unset profile running the default; a profile can be prefixed with a domain; a profile for a test type the domain has no specs of fails as no tests found, one whose directory does not exist stops the container naming the directory, and an unknown profile stops it listing every allowed value and domain, while the domain prefix never reaches the test runner. An active-security profile asked for on the deployed platform is refused, recorded in a failure marker and answered with a report page saying the profile only runs against the compose stack. A run that exits non-zero has its reason appended to that marker and the container exits 1 printing it; a security profile publishes the scan's report directory with the scan's own summary as its index and skips the Allure step, while every other profile publishes the Playwright report, copying it to the configured object store with a zip of its results and failing when the path is unset or the report is missing. A run can be narrowed with the runner's own parameters, and the report is opened or generated by its own commands.
requirements.why: A new suite, domain or test type this programme adds has to be reachable by one of these scripts or profiles, and a chrome change that breaks a run shows up through this entrypoint.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-002 to p16-024 list the scripts and what each leaves out, and p16-135 to p16-151 the deployed profiles, their refusals and how each publishes its report.

requirements.statement: The tests repo holds four domains, each a functional area served by one or more services, and a domain is selected by the directory its specs live in, which also gives them their base URL; a spec outside a known domain directory stops the run naming the four. Within a domain, specs are grouped as accessibility, end-to-end (with feature, page, journey and visual sub-folders) and security folders, but a folder only organises: the test type is selected by one of five tags and a suite is a domain's directory or one test type within it, each path ending in a slash because the runner reads it as a regular expression. A service tag is a different thing: it names a service whose pull request should also run the spec, whatever its test type or domain, and eight are recognised, each belonging to the domains that already run it by path. Linting fails a spec whose tags disagree with its test-type directory, and one that carries the service tag of a service whose pull request already runs its domain by path; the check asks the runner to list the tests so it reads the tags a test really has, names each offending test by file, line and title, and otherwise reports how many it checked. A further tag marks an end-to-end spec whose behaviour a frontend's own suite also proves.
requirements.why: A new spec this programme writes has to sit in the right domain and carry the right tags, or the lint fails it and the pull-request runs either miss it or run it everywhere.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-079 to p16-092 give the domains, the folders, the five type tags, the eight service tags and the lint that enforces them.

requirements.statement: A spec in the tests repo is written to the suite's own conventions. It reaches a page through a named step in its domain's journey file rather than its own clicks, and a sequence two tests share becomes such a step with the local copies deleted; a flow or page object holds no assertion and an assertion two specs share lives in a shared checks module; a journey spec is never seeded, seeding being only for the set-up of a one-page assertion; test data is copied from real canned data and never invented; answers are plain data apart from the steps that drive the pages, in named mandatory and full sets, and a spec starts from a set and overrides single values rather than changing the steps. A spec asserts which page is open through the page object's own URL pattern and never types a trail itself. Support code sits in named folders for specs, flows, page objects, domain constants, fixtures, adapters, canned data and cross-domain helpers, and shared code may not import a domain's page objects, flows or constants. A test title says what its assertions prove and a test must fail without the change it covers. A comment describes only the lines below it and only where a name cannot, the code carries no history, and a spec carries no ticket key, backlog or ruling id, release name or the words 'real service' in a comment, a title or a tag: the lint fails it and tells the author to say what the code does, or what the assertions prove, instead. A catch that drops its error is refused, as is an error or warning logged with only a string while a caught error is in scope; the lint also runs type-checked rules and refuses a floating promise. Lint, the formatting check and the type check run before a commit, with a pre-commit hook on the staged files.
requirements.why: Every new proof this programme writes is reviewed against these rules, and the ban on ticket keys, release names and ruling ids in a spec is why a requirement's words have to say what the behaviour is rather than which decision produced it.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-209 to p16-229 give the lint rules and the code-quality conventions, p16-094 and p16-095 how a spec asserts a page and where a shared assertion lives, and p16-218 to p16-225 the folder layout and the answer sets.

requirements.statement: The tests repo's cross-browser set is existing end-to-end specs selected by one tag and run in branded Chrome, the runner's Firefox and WebKit builds, an emulated iPhone 17 and an emulated Pixel 10, and on a hosted device service against the deployed services on three platforms: the runner's WebKit on the newest macOS, and Safari on the two current iOS versions. A test is tagged only if it runs against the deployed services and renders a page the set does not already cover, chosen so that together the set renders as many pages as possible in each engine, preferring a journey walk and then one test per page the walks do not reach, and leaving out validation, back-end, visual, accessibility and security specs; a tagged test still runs in the default run. A command names its project and adds the tag filter, because a named engine without it would run every test. Edge has no project because it shares Chrome's engine, real iOS Safari is the biggest gap the runner's own builds leave and covers every iPhone browser, and real Android browsers, real Firefox, real macOS Safari and Chrome or Edge on Windows are deliberately not covered, real Android being checked by hand before a release. Session reuse is off on the hosted service because a real iPhone allows one browser context, each platform runs half the machine's processors up to the team limit, the local tunnel cannot open localhost from Safari, WebKit or Android so those platforms run only against the deployed services, network logs are off because they would keep sign-in cookies, and a run stops before starting if either credential is missing. The set is reviewed when the government's own list changes or a new iOS or macOS arrives, against a named propagation list.
requirements.why: A page this programme changes keeps or earns its cross-browser tag under these rules, and the shared chrome is what every tagged test renders.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-168 to p16-183 give the set, how a test is chosen and what is deliberately left out, and p16-184 to p16-193 the hosted service's own rules. The accessible autocomplete adds a hidden position counter on an iPhone user agent, so a spec must not assume a fixed viewport (repo-tests-p16-183).

requirements.statement: The tests repo's Dynamics integration checks, which prove a submitted notification reaches a domain's Dynamics instance through the Dataverse Web API, are not changed by this programme. They run only through their own profile, are left out of every other run, skip on the compose stack, read their settings by function rather than at load so one domain's missing setting cannot fail another's tests, fail at once naming a missing variable and never its value, and are given a longer base timeout; on the deployed platform their calls go through the platform proxy, which must allow the sign-in host and the Dynamics host.
requirements.why: Design and chrome changes reach no Dynamics field, so these checks are weighed where notification publishing is weighed, not here.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-153 to p16-162 describe the suite, its profile, its credentials and its timeouts as they stand.

requirements.statement: The tests repo's own build and delivery stand: a test image built on the official runner image with the London time zone, curl, zip, a Java runtime and the cloud CLI, dependencies installed from the lockfile with lifecycle scripts skipped, run as a non-root user, built for one architecture because of that CLI, and carrying a copied security-scanner install with the add-on that needs a browser profile removed. A push to the default branch builds and publishes the image to both registries, tagged with the computed next version and latest, labelled with the repo, the suite name, the build run and the commit, and commits the version tag; a pull request publishes a branch image through the workspace's branch-publish workflow with a layer cache the main publish writes. End-to-end tests run in continuous integration through the workspace's reusable workflow, which starts the workspace stack probing for the branch's images and runs the published test image against it, publishing reports; that workflow runs only for a pull request whose image publish succeeded or on manual dispatch with a branch to probe, keeps one run per branch, and reports a pending check and then the result back to the pull request. A pull request also runs the formatting check, the lint and the type check, and the same job runs weekly. The dependency audit is a separate job, so a newly published advisory does not gate the merge or block the pull request carrying the fix, and every allowlist entry must carry an advisory id, be active, give a reason and an owner and have a real expiry no more than three months away, an expired entry failing the check. The suite runs on its pinned runtime, is driven by its pinned test runner with the accessibility, reporting, device-service, database and queue clients it declares, pins one transitive dependency for the whole install, clears its previous results and saved sessions at the start of a run, can seed a notification from a script of its own, documents the four workspace commands that start, build, stop and rebuild the stack, publishes its reports and cleans them up when a pull request closes, and is licensed under the Open Government Licence version 3 with its attribution kept.
requirements.why: A chrome change that breaks a run is caught by these checks, and an increment that adds a route or a fixture has to keep the image, the workflows and the audit green.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-194 to p16-208 give the image, the publishes and the workflows, p16-203 and p16-204 the audit's own rules, and p16-265 to p16-271 the pinned runtime, dependencies, seeding script and stack commands.

requirements.statement: A notification belongs to the organisation that created it, and a signed-in user of another organisation reaches none of it. Opening a notification's page by its address shows the standard 404 Page not found page, which leaks neither its Overview heading nor its reference number; on the backend API, reading a submitted notification's fulfilments is refused with 403, every change to a notification (amend, save, submit, copy, soft delete and cancel amend) is refused with 404, and listing notifications by a reference the organisation does not own returns no rows rather than a refusal. The organisation a request acts for is carried on the backend API in its own header.
requirements.why: Organisation scoping is a real authorisation constraint the prototype cannot express, and it is what makes the shared error page the right answer to another organisation's address. It already works and is proven with a real second sign-in.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p6-082 to p6-089 prove the refusals, the header that carries the organisation and the second sign-in the proof uses.

requirements.statement: The animals admin portal's own pages are weighed where the admin portal is weighed, not with the journey services' shared chrome: that a notification submitted in the animals journey is listed there and can be found by its reference, that it reads notifications through the animals backend so finding one there proves the journey app and the admin app agree, and that its replay-all and delete-all banners show only once its call to the gateway has succeeded, which is how its dead-letter specs prove the two are wired together.
requirements.why: The admin portal is a separate internal interface with its own chrome and its own area; this area covers the shared chrome of the journey frontends and the INS front door.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p6-090, p6-091 and p16-262 record the admin portal's own proof as it stands.

requirements.statement: An end-to-end proof that creates an address or a transporter follows the suite's own rules for shared state. Every name it creates carries a timestamp or unique suffix so a search finds only that run's record; the address-book fixtures delete every address and transporter they created when the test ends, pass or fail and on every retry, logging a failed delete with the record's id without failing the test; a transporter saved through the user interface is deleted only if the spec tracks it by name, and an address added on the add-address page or through the cross-service hand-off is not deleted at all. The shared journey addresses are seeded in global set-up through its own client so no test's clean-up removes them, and a spec that edits or deletes an address makes its own record instead. Because the book is shared and never wiped locally, a spec that counts rows searches for a token only its own run created or writes to an organisation whose book starts empty; because the picker lists records newest first and other workers are adding records, a spec that needs a record off page one creates enough newer records to fill page one and then follows Next until its record shows. On the deployed environments addresses expire about seven days after they are created where that is switched on, and the compose stack switches it off. A reset script brings a deployed environment's shared organisation back to a small known state, soft-deleting only records whose name matches a name a test creates, keeping the seeded journey addresses and the performance suite's records, run from a developer's own machine with their API key and never from continuous integration, reporting and deleting nothing by default, deleting addresses only when told to and transporters only when asked, printing the environment and organisation first, refusing production, and reporting in its dry run how many records it would delete and keep with the deletes by name and the commonest kept names.
requirements.why: The address book the navigation leads to is shared state that every worker reads, so a new proof added by this programme has to create, name and clean up its records this way or it breaks other specs.

requirements.statement: How a commodity line is named and found in a test is weighed with the commodity pages, not here: the commodity page's tick-box label of scientific name then common name in brackets under a commodity-code heading, with the scientific name alone where reference data holds no common name; that one scientific name can sit under several commodity codes so a line is identified by code as well as name; that the aggregated notification's commodity label uses the first trade line's description; that the stack's reference-data stub answers only the searches saved from it, the first page of results holds 100 entries and only a species a search showed can be saved, so a seeded journey posts the search first; the constants file naming each line by search term, code, scientific name and common name; and that a spec builds its expected label from that constant or, where it needs the live answer, reads it through the reference-data client and hands it to the same helper.
requirements.why: These are the commodity pages' own content and the reference lists behind them, which the commodities area weighs against the target design and the data specification.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-049 to p16-052 and p16-050-m1 and p16-051-m1 record the labels, the stub's limits and the constants as they stand.

requirements.statement: What the end-to-end suite proves about one page's own content or one journey's own answers is weighed in that page's area, not here: that a brand-new notification opens at the origin page with nothing answered and the entry guard admits it on an answer the trader entered; the arrival date's window and its unpadded display form and a temporary admission's later exit date; how an accompanying document is added and waited for and the budgets its list and scan are given; the import reason's conditional purpose; the transporter pages' order, their add forms, where each save lands, and why two tests adding a transporter of the same name can refuse a list's save; the overview's two sets of task rows in their fixed order; the rail, cat and poultry consignments' own answers and where each walk ends; the permanent address page's place in the journey; what the animals API seed unlocks; a party picker's refusal of a record without the role, its server round trip and how a party's row and a summary card's links and subsections are found; the review page's own slug and the cancel-amend page's; how a species tick box and a transit port of exit are chosen; and every named walk a spec starts from.
requirements.why: This area stops at any one page's own content and answers; those pages' areas weigh the same behaviours against the target design and the data specification.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-232 to p16-260 and repo-frontend-p2-049, p2-133, p2-135 and p2-136 record those pages' own behaviour and the suite's facts about them as they stand.

requirements.statement: Every page of every frontend is rendered and usable before any script runs: the service stylesheet loads in the head and the service script loads as a module at the end of the body, and the stylesheet is built from GOV.UK Frontend plus the Ministry of Justice date picker and search components before the service's own variables, helpers, core, components and partials. Where JavaScript runs, the pages get the GOV.UK button, tick box, error summary, radio, service navigation and skip-link behaviours, the Ministry of Justice date picker, and the service's own enhancements, and nothing else: a behaviour is built from GOV.UK Frontend first, then another tested government library, and otherwise goes back to design. Anything a page can only offer with JavaScript is hidden when the GOV.UK JavaScript has not run, so a trader without it is never shown a control that would do nothing, and nothing a trader needs is shown only by script.
requirements.why: The owner's 9 October afternoon ruling makes every page work fully without JavaScript, with CSS and JavaScript only enhancing a page that already works, and limits the libraries a behaviour may come from. Both journey frontends already load their assets and hide their script-only controls this way.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-frontend-p2-028 and repo-plantsfrontend-p13-030 load the stylesheet and the script so a page is usable first, repo-frontend-p2-111, p2-112 and p2-124 and repo-plantsfrontend-p13-095 list the libraries and hide the script-only controls, and the ruling holds every page to working without JavaScript (ruling-sam-2026-10-09-pm-p1-033).

requirements.statement: The shared search box, the multi-select search, the transporter filter, the country dialling prefix and the page-specific styling of lists, totals and icon buttons are weighed where the pages that use them are weighed, not with the shared chrome: the autocomplete over a native select with its options, its matching that ignores capitals and accents, its bold matched letters, its square blue magnifier hidden from assistive technology, its assistive hint and Welsh announcements, its typography, focus and error borders and its pinned upstream licence; the multi-select search's ticked results, its server-rendered matching, its refresh timing, queueing, focus handling and announcements, its fall back to a plain form post, its no-JavaScript update button and its bordered result list with chips and Clear all; the seven long-list fields of the live-animals journey and how each is proven, with and without JavaScript, at phone width and against a real GOV.UK input; the transporter list's in-page filter with its announcements; the prefix that changes with the country; the live region announced a moment after a page loads; and the notification list's filter panel and toolbar, the commodity totals panel, the service's icon button styling, a task row's status staying on one line while a long hint wraps, a table cell holding an unbroken reference breaking rather than widening the table, and the red bar down a summary card with answers still outstanding.
requirements.why: Each of these is one page's own control or one page's own styling, and the pages' areas weigh them against the target design, the owner's ruling that a search box uses the accessible autocomplete with the reference list's own entries, and the rule that the version without JavaScript is built first.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-frontend-p2-078 to p2-110 and p2-138 to p2-150 record the search controls and their proof as they stand, and p2-117, p2-121 and p2-123 the page-specific styling.

requirements.statement: On the animals frontend a date is asked for in one box about ten characters wide, as day/month/year text with a small label and the Ministry of Justice date picker beside it. A date is read as day, month and year only when it is one or two digits, a slash, one or two digits, a slash and four digits; anything else is kept as typed and shown back to the trader. The picker's calendar opens below the field rather than floating over the page, at most 360 pixels wide, and its toggle is a blue icon button.
requirements.why: This is the shared date field of the animals page kit, the same field plants has, and the interaction designer's 9 November answers keep the Ministry of Justice picker for every date in both frontends.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-frontend-p2-114 to p2-116 describe the field and its picker, and the interaction designer keeps that picker as the one every date already uses (ruling-interaction-designer-2026-11-09-p1-040).

requirements.statement: On the animals frontend, a journey page's primary button reads 'Save and continue' unless the page gives the shared save controls its own primary label and styling, and beside it sit a secondary 'Save and return to overview' button and, below them, a 'Cancel and return to overview' link to the notification's overview. A page can leave out both return controls and show only its primary button, and can add one more secondary button of its own beside the save controls, posting its own name and value. On a page that takes a file, every save button posts the form to the upload path as multipart, so a chosen file is sent whichever save the trader presses, and a page can put a hidden implicit-submit control ahead of its other buttons so pressing Enter in a field activates the control the page intends. Pressing 'Save and return to overview' on any journey page goes to that notification's overview; pressing 'Save and continue' goes to the next page of the journey that applies to the notification, to the review page when none is left, and to the page that asks for a required earlier answer the notification does not have when the next page needs one.
requirements.why: These are the animals frontend's shared save controls, the twin of the plants ones, and the owner's 26 October ruling makes both save buttons run the same checks on every page that has them.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-frontend-p2-034 to p2-040 give the controls and the two ways a page varies them, and p2-046 to p2-048 where each save lands.

requirements.statement: The accessibility suite scans the INS front door and its address book: the blank address-type question, the blank add-address form, the add form fully entered with an optional second address line, a county and its roles ticked, an address's view page for a record with the required fields only and again for one with the extra fields, the edit form filled with a stored address, the delete confirmation, the address-type question, the add form and the edit form each with their error summary showing, the populated list and the list with the success banner after an address is added, the list's second page reached by seeding nine addresses and following Next, the dashboard in its default populated and sorted views, the dashboard with a search that matches a reference and again with one that matches nothing, the dashboard's paginated view where there is more than one page, the sign-in page on first load from a cold session and again with an error, and the unauthorised page. The address book's and the dashboard's longer pages are scanned again at both narrow viewports.
requirements.why: The INS front door and the address book are where the navigation leads, and every page this programme changes there must keep passing these scans.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p15-061 to p15-079 define the INS scans, the states each covers and the two narrow viewports.

conflicts.about: Whether the service navigation keeps a Log out item: the target design drops it, and the deployed services have it.

positions.says: In DR2.1 the service navigation has no Log out item, unlike design release 2.
A real constraint the prototype cannot express, such as authentication, overrides the prototype default.
DR1 judged that sign-out sits in the service navigation as 'Log out', replacing the separate 'Sign out' link.
The Log out navigation link signs the user out at /auth/sign-out.

conflicts.outcome: Log out stays as the last navigation item on every frontend: both animals sets, the INS frontend and the plants frontend (req-969, req-1674, req-965). The prototype has no real session to end, so leaving it out does not show a decision about sign-out. In the deployed services, Log out is the only way to end a Defra ID session, and the ruling lets an authentication constraint override the prototype. The rest of the prototype's list (Dashboard, Templates, Address book, Manage account) is adopted, so prototype-dr2-1-source-p1-021 and p1-018 still back the Templates requirement. Only the claim that drops Log out is set aside.

conflicts.about: Where the Address book navigation item goes: inside the same service in the target design, or the INS frontend's address book in the deployed services.

positions.says: Under DR2.1 the address book sits under the service's own base path, at /design-release-2.1/address-book.
Rhys ruled that the dashboard and the address book are temporary in the animals frontend and move to trade-imports-ins-frontend.
Cross-service behaviour the prototype cannot express overrides the prototype default.
The prototype never decides architecture: the split into services and URL paths stay the deployed services'.
c-213 is kept for a real constraint or a DR1 judgement.

conflicts.outcome: The Address book item goes to the INS frontend's address book from the animals frontend, in both animals sets, and from the INS frontend (req-1677). The address book is a shared capability in a separate service, which the single-service prototype cannot express, and the owner's later ruling keeps this conflict and says the prototype never decides services or URL paths. The prototype claim that places it under the service's own base is set aside. The item, its label and its place in the order still stand. Plants is not wired to the INS address book, so its item keeps the destination its page context supplies (req-2084). Rhys's DR1 judgement still moves the address book to the INS frontend, though the 9 October afternoon and templates rulings keep the notification lists in their own frontends (c-314).

conflicts.about: Where the GOV.UK header logo and the service name link: the target design sends both to its index of design releases, which has no counterpart in a deployed service.

positions.says: The GOV.UK logo links to the service index (/design-release-2.1/index), and the service name in the service navigation does too.
On DR2.1 pages the header logo and the service name both link to the prototype index.
The GOV.UK header's crown links to https://www.gov.uk/.
The service name in the navigation links to the page's home URL, which on a journey page is the set's own notification list.
The GOV.UK header logo links to https://www.gov.uk/.
A question for people is raised only when a difference is truly exceptional and neither the prototype default nor a DR1 judgement settles it.
c-214 is kept for a real constraint or a DR1 judgement.

conflicts.outcome: Keep the current targets, as the owner's later ruling confirms. The GOV.UK logo links to https://www.gov.uk/ on every frontend, as the GOV.UK header pattern does. The service name links to the dashboard home of the set or frontend the page belongs to: the live-animals set's root on live-animals pages, the germinal set's root on germinal-products pages, the plants set's root on plants pages and / on the INS frontend. Each set root renders its own notification list (c-314). The prototype sends both links to its index of design releases, which is prototype tooling that is not built (req-1681), so it names no real destination to move them to; the prototype keeps a separate Dashboard item, so its index is not a stand-in for the dashboard. With no DR1 judgement on the header links, the deployed frontends' targets are the only buildable ones and stand.

conflicts.about: Where the phase banner's feedback link goes: a placeholder '#' in the target design, or the APHA service desk mailbox in the deployed services.

positions.says: DR2.1 dashboard pages show an Alpha phase banner whose feedback link is a placeholder '#'.
Because the design's feedback link is a placeholder, DR1 ruled it to be mailto:APHAServiceDesk@apha.gov.uk, and forbade inventing a /feedback route or survey URL.
The phase banner's feedback link opens an email to the APHA service desk.

conflicts.outcome: The feedback link stays mailto:APHAServiceDesk@apha.gov.uk on every frontend, plants included (req-1684). DR1 already judged this same difference, a placeholder feedback link in the design, and a DR1 judgement on the same difference outranks the prototype. The INS and plants frontends already use the same destination. The Alpha banner itself is shown by today's claims (req-956), so setting aside the prototype's placeholder claim loses nothing.

conflicts.about: Whether service pages show the signed-in user's email and Home and About links, as the tests repo's shared page object suggests.

positions.says: The layout does not show the signed-in user's name or email anywhere, although the view context supplies a display name.
No page shows the signed-in user's name or email address, and there is no user header band.

Open: the end-to-end tests still look for a 'Sign out' link and the signed-in email on the notification dashboard, and the action was to point sign-out at 'Log out' and delete the test that displays the signed-in user.
The signed-in identity strip was removed, so the service no longer shows the signed-in user's email or display name, matching the design, which shows no signed-in identity.

conflicts.outcome: No page shows the signed-in identity (req-1702). The frontends outrank the tests repo: the INS and plants layouts show no name or email, the end-to-end traces show none (trace-e2e-p1-040) and the tests repo's own dashboard spec asserts no email (repo-tests-p6-074). What the shared page object once suggested was a stale helper no spec asserted, and the tests repo's slice of this area no longer carries a claim that any page shows an identity, so nothing is listed as overruled; the open item that the suite still looked for a 'Sign out' link and the email is answered by the same outcome, and the locators can go whenever the tests repo is next touched.

conflicts.about: What the status strip calls an AMEND notification: 'Amending', as both journey frontends showed, or 'Amend'.

positions.says: The shared strip's 'Amending' label changes to 'Amend' in every set at once.
Plants' status strip tag reads Amend in yellow for a notification being amended.
The security walk checks a notification being amended by the status reading Amend.

conflicts.outcome: The strip reads 'Amend' in every set, plants included, through the one shared strip (req-2061). The owner's ruling outranked both journey frontends' earlier 'Amending' label, and since then both have taken it: the animals and plants strips and the plants Welsh twin now read 'Amend' and 'Diwygio', and the security walk reads the status as Amend, so nothing is left to build. Nothing is overruled, because the frontend and tests claims now record the ruling's own wording rather than contradicting it. The notification list card's own tag is not named by the ruling and stays as the list area has it.

conflicts.about: What proves a plants page this programme changes, given the plants domain has end-to-end and visual specs only and no accessibility or security specs.

positions.says: Where plants has the same page or behaviour, the same increment changes plants too.
The plants domain has docker-compose scripts for end-to-end and visual only, and none for accessibility or security.
No attacking spec exists for the high-risk plants journey, so the plants backend is declared as a context with an attack job of its own that nothing drives.
Neither the per-domain script table nor the profile table says whether plants' missing accessibility and security suites are planned or deliberately out of scope.

conflicts.outcome: Nothing ranks the two readings. The owner's rule that plants takes the same change in the same increment can be read as carrying the animals proof across, which would mean writing plants an accessibility suite and a security corpus, or as carrying only the change, which leaves a changed plants page proved by the end-to-end and visual specs it has. Neither the rulings nor the tests repo's own documentation settles it, so it goes to the owner with a default.
conflicts.question: When an increment changes a plants page as well as an animals one, does plants get accessibility and security specs for that page, or is its end-to-end and visual proof enough?
conflicts.default: Animals and INS pages keep their existing accessibility and security suites. A plants page this programme changes is proved by the plants domain's end-to-end and visual specs and by the plants frontend's own in-repo checks, and no plants accessibility specs or attacking security specs are written; the full attacking run keeps failing its no-traffic gate on the plants backend context, so only per-domain attacking runs are used, and that gap goes to the report.
